actuation: Motor-driven linear stage powered by a stepper motor (Oriental Motor PKP235D23A) coupled with a timing belt pulley and a threaded rod
constitutive_assumptions: Linear elasticity formulation in the topology optimization framework relating element stiffness matrix linearly to equivalent elastic modulus (k_i = E_i * k_0)

Metamaterial homogenization assumption where 3D-printed infill structures with periodic cells and varied infill percentages represent isotropic equivalent elastic moduli (e.g., 100% infill = 34.95 MPa, 40% infill = 14.46 MPa, void = Emin)
Numerical spring stiffness k applied at input and target output ports to formulate mutual potential energy
control_variables: Initial spacing between the two fingers (60 mm in initial state)

3D-printing material (commercial TPE filament Filastic by BotFeeder) and printing parameters (rectilinear infill pattern, nozzle temperature 220 °C, platform temperature 50 °C, print speed 20 mm/s, layer thickness 0.2 mm)
Actuator hardware and transmission (Oriental Motor PKP235D23A stepper motor, linear stage, timing belt pulley, threaded rod)
Diameter of aluminum test cylinder used in payload experiments (76.1 mm)
dependent_variables: Input actuation force required for a given input displacement (N)
Total contact length between the fingers and the grasped object (measured in pixels and contact length ratio)
Conformal grasping success across irregular, asymmetric, thin, wide, and delicate objects

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Dividing a compliant finger into multiple phalanges connected by flexure hinges and synthesizing each domain via multi-material topology optimization yields increased fingertip output displacement and reduced actuation force.

The multi-infill density compliant finger produces an average output displacement roughly 9% larger than single-infill density fingers of comparable weight, reaching approximately 1.16 times the output displacement at 30 mm input displacement.

The multi-infill density finger requires 12.4% and 23.2% lower average input force compared to single-infill density fingers of 90% and 100%, respectively, while avoiding the excessive buckling observed in the low-stiffness 40% infill design.

Using total contact length as an adaptability metric for circular, rectangular, trapezoidal, and concave objects, the multi-infill density gripper exhibited an average contact length 1.5 times that of the Festo MultiChoiceGripper, successfully conforming to all four geometries.

In hanging payload tests using a 76.1 mm diameter cylinder, the multi-infill density gripper achieved a maximum payload of 6.76 kg, outperforming a 100% infill finger design (5.35 kg) and a Festo Fin Ray gripper (2.45 kg, achieving 2.8 times its capacity).

The highly self-adaptive gripper successfully gripped diverse challenging objects including 3D-printed asymmetric shapes, a concave shape, food items (apple, raw egg, mango), a balloon, a thin plate, and an object 128 mm wide (88% of maximum fingertip distance).

experimental_setup: Finger deformation test setup: A linear stage actuated the finger input port while a force gauge recorded input force across displacements, with fingertip displacement tracked and compared to LS-DYNA FEA simulations.

Two-fingered soft robotic gripper: Two identical 3D-printed multi-phalange compliant fingers (fabricated via Raise3D printer with BotFeeder Filastic TPE) mounted on a linear stage driven by a stepper motor (Oriental Motor PKP235D23A) with timing belt pulley and threaded rod.

Adaptability assessment: Grasping experiments on four canonical geometric shapes (circular, rectangular, trapezoidal, and concave); contact interfaces were photographed and quantified via pixel counts using ImageJ software.
Payload evaluation: Gripping a 76.1 mm diameter hollow aluminum cylinder with a suspended mass tray, adding mass incrementally until grasp failure to determine maximum load capacity.
Practical grasping verification: Grasping trials on 11 distinct everyday and custom objects spanning irregular 3D contours, deformable bodies, delicate eggs, thin plates, and wide objects.
independent_variables: Finger structural design and infill configuration (multi-infill density finger vs. 100%, 90%, and 40% single-infill fingers vs. Festo Fin Ray gripper)
Input displacement applied by the linear stage (ranging from 0 mm to 30 mm)
Object geometry and profile (circular, rectangular, trapezoidal, concave, asymmetric, thin, and wide up to 128 mm)
Mass loaded onto the suspended tray during payload capacity testing
limitations_inferred: The design optimization and structural kinematics are purely planar (2D extrusion of 20 mm), which limits compliance and contact adaptation along the out-of-plane dimension for complex 3D spherical or contoured surfaces.

Actuation is purely open-loop kinematic displacement with a single actuator; no tactile, proximity, or closed-loop contact force sensors are integrated to regulate contact pressure on fragile objects.
Viscoelastic effects such as creep, stress relaxation, and fatigue durability under repeated high-load grasping cycles were not evaluated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Comparisons with the Festo MultiChoiceGripper may not be entirely fair due to disparities in materials, friction coefficients, actuation mechanisms, and motor power.
A compliant finger printed entirely with a 40% infill density exhibited insufficient stiffness, making it prone to excessive deformation and structural buckling during grasping.

The third intermediate material phase (E2) occupied an extremely small fraction of the optimized layout and was omitted from the physical prototype for manufacturing feasibility, leaving a bi-material (40% and 100% infill) final structure.
The maximum graspable object width was constrained to 128 mm, representing approximately 88% of the maximum fingertip separation distance.
main_results: The multi-infill density compliant finger produced roughly 9% higher average output displacement than single-infill density fingers, achieving 1.16 times the fingertip displacement at 30 mm input displacement.
The multi-infill density finger reduced required input actuation force by 12.4% and 23.2% on average relative to 90% and 100% single-infill fingers, respectively.

The multi-infill density gripper conformed to circular (543 px), rectangular (522 px), trapezoidal (570 px), and concave (538 px) objects, averaging 1.5 times the total contact length of the Festo Fin Ray gripper.

The multi-infill density gripper supported a maximum load capacity of 6.76 kg, which is 1.26 times that of the 100% infill design (5.35 kg) and 2.8 times that of the Festo MultiChoiceGripper (2.45 kg).
The gripper successfully conformed to and grasped 11 diverse test objects ranging from asymmetric 3D shapes to delicate eggs, balloons, thin plates, and wide objects up to 128 mm.
modeling_methods: Three-material density-based topology optimization maximizing mutual potential energy (MPE) under volume fraction constraints using the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA)
Density filtering and projection schemes incorporating robust eroded, intermediate, and dilated formulations to account for manufacturing tolerances
Finite Element Analysis (FEA) using LS-DYNA to simulate finger deformation contours, input force curves, and output displacement curves
Digital image analysis via ImageJ to compute pixel coordinates and measure total contact length between fingers and objects
performance_metrics: Total contact length (pixels) and contact length ratio relative to Festo design
Maximum graspable object dimension (mm and % of maximum fingertip opening)
possible_gap_implications: The combination of multi-material topology optimization, metamaterial infill tuning, and flexure hinges successfully enhances payload and in-plane adaptability, but does not address out-of-plane conformity or 3D spatial grasping demands.

Future research could explore embedding distributed tactile sensing or closed-loop grasping force regulation within topology-optimized multi-density metamaterial fingers to prevent damage to fragile objects under motor-driven actuation.
paper.research_objective: To design, synthesize, and experimentally evaluate a highly self-adaptive compliant robotic gripper with multi-material, multi-phalange fingers connected by flexure hinges and fabricated using 3D-printed variable-density infill metamaterials to achieve high shape adaptability and high payload capacity for irregularly shaped objects.
paper.research_problem: Developing robotic grippers that can handle objects of varying sizes, shapes, weights, and hardness without excessive actuator count, control complexity, or bulk, while overcoming the payload capacity limitations typically encountered in soft compliant grippers.
stiffness_mechanism: varying 3D-printed infill densities (metamaterial approach with periodic cells of 40% and 100% infill)
flexure hinges connecting multi-material compliant phalanges
paper.title: Optimal Design of a Highly Self-Adaptive Gripper with Multi-Phalange Compliant Fingers for Grasping Irregularly Shaped Objects
